chunks: Changing I2C rise time. The question: How do you increase rise time on I2C?
I2C is a two-wire connection that lets chips talk. When no chip is pulling a wire low, a resistor pulls it back up to the supply voltage.
The "rise time" is how long that climb takes. Careful: "increase the rise time", taken literally, means make the climb slower.
People almost always mean the opposite: the climb is too slow, and they want a shorter rise time. Say which one you mean, answer that usual case first, then cover the other.
Think of a bucket filled from a tap through a hose. The bucket is the wire's stored charge. A narrow hose (a big resistor) fills it slowly.
A wide hose (a small resistor) fills it fast. A bigger bucket (more wire and more chips attached) takes longer.
The analogy misses one limit: with a wider hose, a chip must swallow more current to pull the wire low.
At the default 100 picofarads, the 30%–70% rise times are 847 nanoseconds (10 kilohms), 398 nanoseconds (4. 7 kilohms), 186 nanoseconds (2.
2 kilohms) and 85 nanoseconds (1 kilohms). 10 kilohms meets Standard mode only; 4. 7 kilohms misses Fast mode's 300 nanoseconds; 2. 2 kilohms passes with margin.
Drag C b up to 200 picofarads: the 2. 2 kilohms pull-up then takes about 373 nanoseconds and misses Fast mode, while 1 kilohms (170 nanoseconds) still passes.
Rise time: how long the wire takes to go from 30% to 70% of the supply voltage after a chip lets go. Pull-up resistor: the resistor from the wire to the supply that pulls it high.
Bus capacitance: how much charge the wire and its attached parts soak up as the voltage changes. Sink current: how much current a chip can absorb while holding the wire low.
A good estimate is rise time about 0. 85 times R times C . Take a 10 kilohms pull-up and 100 picofarads of capacitance.
That gives about 850 nanoseconds (nanoseconds, billionths of a second). A bus running at 400 kilohertz needs 300 nanoseconds or less, so that is too slow. Swap in a 2.
2 kilohms resistor and the time drops to about 190 nanoseconds. Removing capacitance helps the same way. That is the whole idea.
"I'd clarify the direction, but assuming I want it faster: rise time is about 0. 85 times R p times C b , so I lower R p , down to the sink-current limit of about 970 ohms at 3.
3 volts, or I reduce capacitance with shorter traces, fewer devices, or a mux. If the window is closed I use a rise-time accelerator or current-source pull-up, or slow down.
To make it slower on purpose I'd do the opposite, a bigger resistor or a small series R."
